curriculum.lesson_evidence: Perspectives in history are viewpoints shaped by role, time and purpose. Contestability means historians can disagree when evidence is incomplete. Empathy means trying to understand past viewpoints without excusing harm; fair representation includes groups often missing from elite sources.
curriculum.scope_limit: Proposed Stage 4 NESA HSIE alignment using catalogue outcome code HT4-1; content-point mapping remains pending. Local First Nations protocols and Community verification remain pending human review. Do not invent Country names, Dreaming stories, sacred knowledge or unverified cultural claims.

lesson.child_mission: Perspectives in history are viewpoints shaped by role, time and purpose. Contestability means historians can disagree when evidence is incomplete. Empathy means trying to understand past viewpoints without excusing harm; fair representation includes groups often missing from elite sources.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same HSIE idea to a new place or source, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Give two contrasting perspectives on one ancient event from class sources and one reason they might differ.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: Perspectives evidenced; difference explained by authorship/purpose/audience.

WATCH FOR
Picking one source as the only truth. Multiple perspectives need weighing.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Write a short contested-interpretation paragraph: claim A, claim B, shared evidence, remaining uncertainty.

Write a short reflection naming one source or idea you corrected and why.

lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Write a short contested-interpretation paragraph: claim A, claim B, shared evidence, remaining uncertainty. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original response on new material: Strong answer: Perspectives evidenced; difference explained by authorship/purpose/audience. Reasoning: I used perspective by attending to contestability rather than copying the worked model.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Picking one source as the only truth. Multiple perspectives need weighing. Correction: Strong answer: Perspectives evidenced; difference explained by authorship/purpose/audience. Why: the correction restores accurate use of perspective.

Parent: Likely misconception: Picking one source as the only truth. Multiple perspectives need weighing. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Produce a fresh example demonstrating perspective on new material (not the worked model). Explain the particular words, sources or choices that make it work.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with perspective, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Example: A royal inscription celebrating a victory and a later Greek account of the same war may differ. Historians cross-check and note gaps for non-elite people.

TRY FIRST
Give two contrasting perspectives on one ancient event from class sources and one reason they might differ.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: Perspectives evidenced; difference explained by authorship/purpose/audience.
teach_steps.explain:
Perspectives in history are viewpoints shaped by role, time and purpose. Contestability means historians can disagree when evidence is incomplete. Empathy means trying to understand past viewpoints without excusing harm; fair representation includes groups often missing from elite sources.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on sources, places and respectful community knowledge, rather than guessing from a single picture. Keep every claim linked to evidence.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the sources, map features or community examples that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a detail is uncertain, identify what source you would need next. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
teach_steps.notice: Picking one source as the only truth. Multiple perspectives need weighing. Correct the claim or use of sources, not just the neatness of the poster.
